prompt: What does `git log` record about a change to `prompts/triage.txt`, and what does it leave out?
hint: Read the subjects again.

choices.text: What changed and when; it leaves out why
choices.why: Right. Every subject describes its diff and none gives a reason.

choices.text: Why it changed; it leaves out the date
choices.why: The dates are there; the reasons are not.

choices.text: The score before and after; it leaves out the author
choices.why: Git knows nothing about scores; `pl log` computes them.

choices.text: Nothing at all about prompt files, which it treats differently from source code
choices.why: Git tracks a prompt file like any other file.

prompt: A new teammate finds the JSON examples hard to read and wants to rewrite them as plain lines. Why will the history probably not stop them?
hint: Who reads a log looking for a reason not to do something?

choices.text: The revert deleted the earlier commit from the history
choices.why: Both commits are still in the log.

choices.text: A log is not read before edits
choices.why: Right: the reason has to sit where a reader of the prompt will find it.

choices.text: Git hides commits older than three months
choices.why: It hides nothing.

choices.text: Plain lines are a better format
choices.why: They took the score to zero.

prompt: Match each note to the question it answers.
hint: Three notes, three questions.

pairs.right: What has gone wrong before, and what stops it again?
What is this, how good is it and what does it cost?

right_distractors: Who is allowed to merge a change?

prompt: Why does the lesson keep these notes beside the prompt rather than in long commit messages?
hint: Who reads each?

choices.text: Git limits a commit message to one line
choices.why: A commit message may have a body of any length.

choices.text: Commit messages cannot hold numbers
choices.why: They can hold anything text can.

choices.text: Commit messages are deleted when a change is reverted, while a note beside the prompt survives that
choices.why: A revert adds a commit; the old message stays.

choices.text: Whoever opens the prompt reads a file beside it; the log is read by somebody already searching
choices.why: Right. A message is scattered across history; a note is where the reader is.

prompt: Where does the form of a decision record come from, as the lesson tells it?
hint: A post from 2011.

choices.text: A machine learning paper about how to evaluate models and report their results to users
choices.why: That is the model card's precedent, not this one.

choices.text: Software architecture: one small numbered file per decision, kept with the code
choices.why: Right: Michael Nygard's Documenting Architecture Decisions.

choices.text: Git's own documentation
choices.why: Git has no notion of a decision.

choices.text: A legal requirement
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

prompt: Why does the record list the options that lost, with their numbers?
hint: Who will propose them again?

choices.text: To make the record look thorough
choices.why: Each part is there for a reader, not for appearance.

choices.text: Because a record must have at least three options
choices.why: There is no minimum; there were three real ones here.

choices.text: The rejected option is what the next person proposes, and here they find it was tried
choices.why: Right. Plain-line examples are the February proposal, and the record answers it.

choices.text: So that `pl log` can read them
choices.why: `pl log` reads git history, not notes.

prompt: The part of a decision record that names the conditions under which the decision would become wrong is headed `Revisit ___`.
hint: Two words in the heading; one is missing.

prompt: A decision recorded last year is reversed today. What does the lesson say to do with the old record?
hint: Nygard's rule.

choices.text: Edit it so that it states the new decision instead
choices.why: That erases the reasoning that was replaced.

choices.text: Delete it
choices.why: The old reasoning is evidence for whoever reads the new one.

choices.text: Leave it exactly as it is and say nothing about the change
choices.why: Then two records disagree and nobody knows which holds.

choices.text: Mark it superseded and write a new one
choices.why: Right: the old reasoning stays readable and the new one explains the change.

prompt: Which of these changes deserves a decision record rather than a sentence in its commit message?
hint: A record is for a real choice that a reasonable person would undo.

choices.text: Fixing a typo in the summary instruction
choices.why: Nobody would choose the typo back.

choices.text: Keeping the examples' order after measuring three orders that scored differently
choices.why: Right: there were options, there is evidence, and somebody will want to reorder them.

choices.text: Escaping the message against closing tags, a change that moved no score on any test set
choices.why: The lesson says that one needed a sentence in its commit message.

choices.text: Renaming the file's variable
choices.why: No choice between alternatives worth recording.

prompt: According to the lesson, what is a failure log entry about?
hint: The idea taken from postmortems.

choices.text: The person who made the edit
choices.why: It is written without blame.

choices.text: The system, not a person
choices.why: Right. Blame teaches people to hide failures.

choices.text: The customer whose message failed
choices.why: The message is evidence; the entry is about the prompt.

choices.text: Only the cost of the incident
choices.why: Cost is one line of nine.

prompt: According to `pl log`, how many tokens did the forty dev calls use under `31a6a59`?
hint: The `tokens` column on that commit's line.

prompt: A customer message is answered wrongly in production, and the prompt is fixed. What finishes the fix, according to the lesson?
hint: What would the gate fail on next time?

choices.text: Thanking the customer
choices.why: Good manners, but nothing stops the failure returning.

choices.text: A note in the commit message, saying what went wrong and why
choices.why: A note does not make the gate fail.

choices.text: Raising the temperature, so that the reply comes out different next time
choices.why: That changes the answers, not the tests.

choices.text: The message, cleaned, added as a case with its right answer
choices.why: Right: otherwise the same failure can come back and pass every check.

prompt: In an entry, the line `Caught by` reads *nothing would have*. Why does the lesson call that the most important line?
hint: What does it say about the tests?

choices.text: It means the failure was harmless, since no check ever noticed it happening
choices.why: A failure nothing catches is the opposite of harmless.

choices.text: It marks a hole in the tests that the next change would fall through
choices.why: Right. Filling it is the test you add.

choices.text: It shows the model is broken
choices.why: It shows the checks are incomplete, whatever the model.

choices.text: It lets the entry be closed early
choices.why: It is the reason the entry needs more work.

prompt: Which published idea does the prompt card follow?
hint: Mitchell and others, 2019.

choices.text: Model cards
choices.why: Right: intended use, evaluation, limitations.

choices.text: Decision records
choices.why: Those come from software architecture, and answer a different question.

choices.text: Postmortems after incidents
choices.why: Those are the failure log's precedent.

choices.text: Release notes
choices.why: The lesson does not cite them.

prompt: The card shows dev 36/40 and holdout 11/30. Why does the lesson call the holdout score the most important line?
hint: What would a reader conclude from the dev number alone?

choices.text: Holdout has fewer messages, so it is more precise
choices.why: Fewer messages make a score less precise, not more.

choices.text: Holdout is the only set the gate runs
choices.why: The gate runs every set.

choices.text: Without it the card would be true and still mislead every reader
choices.why: Right: 36 of 40 reads as finished, and the harder messages say it is not.

choices.text: Holdout scores are always lower, so they look more honest to whoever reads the card
choices.why: It matters because of what it measures, not how it looks.

prompt: `pl cost` reports 5.8032 cents for the forty dev calls. What is the cost of one call, in cents?
hint: Divide by the number of calls.

prompt: Why should the card carry the prompt id and the commit?
hint: A card is a claim about one version.

choices.text: Because the harness refuses to run a prompt without a card
choices.why: The harness knows nothing about cards.

choices.text: So that a reader sees at once whether it describes the file in front of them
choices.why: Right. A stale card looks exactly like a current one otherwise.

choices.text: For billing
choices.why: Cost is on the card, but the id is about identity.

choices.text: To make the card longer
choices.why: Every line is there for a reader.

prompt: Which of these belong on the card, as the lesson writes it? Choose all that apply.
hint: One page for somebody using the prompt.

choices.text: What the prompt is not for
choices.why: Yes: it states the edges of what was tested.

choices.text: The score on every test set
choices.why: Yes, the unflattering ones included.

choices.text: The known failure modes, by message
choices.why: Yes: `t14`, `t24`, `t28` and `t37` on dev.

choices.text: The full text of every earlier version
choices.why: That is what git is for; the card is one page.

prompt: A customer's message is sorted wrongly in production. Put the steps in the order the lesson implies.
hint: The case comes before the fix, so the gate can prove the fix.
items: Add the message, cleaned, as a case with the right answer
Change the prompt until the gate passes, with nothing broken
Write the failure log entry, naming the fix and the case
Update the card's scores in the same change

prompt: A teammate proposes removing the three examples to save tokens. Which note should they read first, and what will it tell them?
hint: The option was considered.

choices.text: The prompt card, which says the prompt is cheap enough already
choices.why: The card gives the cost, not the reason for the examples.

choices.text: The failure log, which says examples never fail
choices.why: F-0001 is a failure caused by examples.

choices.text: Decision 0001: no examples was option 1, at 24 of 40
choices.why: Right: the rejected option is on the record with its number.

choices.text: None: the git log already explains the examples in full
choices.why: The log says what, not why.
